clinicalPearls: A diffuse, boggy swelling of the fetal scalp caused by pressure during delivery
The swelling crosses suture lines, distinguishing it from a cephalohaematoma
It is present at birth and typically resolves within a few days
It may be associated with overlying bruising or petechiae and, with vacuum delivery, a chignon
Because it lies above the periosteum and crosses sutures, it does not cause the significant blood loss seen in subgaleal haemorrhage
Management is expectant, with reassurance to parents
reference.pathophysiology: Caput succedaneum is oedema of the scalp soft tissues, in the subcutaneous layer above the periosteum, produced by pressure from the cervix and birth canal (or a vacuum cup) against the presenting part. This pressure impedes venous and lymphatic return, causing serosanguinous fluid to accumulate diffusely in the scalp. Because the fluid is superficial and not confined by periosteal attachments, it crosses suture lines and resolves quickly as the fluid is reabsorbed.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the diffuse swelling crossing sutures
Assessment for associated bruising and jaundice risk
Distinguishing it from subgaleal haemorrhage, which is more diffuse, fluctuant and dangerous
redFlags: A rapidly enlarging, fluctuant swelling suggesting subgaleal haemorrhage
Signs of significant blood loss or shock
A swelling with a bony defect or pulsation suggesting a congenital lesion
reference.prognosis: Caput succedaneum is benign and resolves spontaneously within days without sequelae.
pitfalls: Mistaking a dangerous subgaleal haemorrhage for benign caput
Confusing it with a cephalohaematoma (which is confined by sutures)
Overlooking associated jaundice from resorbing blood
Unnecessary investigation of a clearly benign swelling
management: Expectant management, as the scalp oedema reabsorbs spontaneously over a few days
Parental reassurance and explanation of the benign, self-limiting nature
Routine observation of the swelling for expected resolution, distinguishing it from a cephalohaematoma and subgaleal haemorrhage
Monitoring for and management of neonatal jaundice arising from resorption of associated bruising
Standard newborn care without imaging or intervention
Escalation if the swelling is unexpectedly fluctuant, enlarging or accompanied by haemodynamic instability, suggesting subgaleal haemorrhage
